newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crippled Mir starts unloading repair supplies.
newsitem.headline: Crippled Mir starts unloading repair supplies.

text.p: Three cosmonauts aboard Russia's Mir space station began unloading vital equipment from a docked supply craft on Tuesday to repair the station damaged by the worst accident in its history, officials said.

The unmanned Progress craft contains oxygen, food, water and tools needed to repair the Spektr module's energy-generating solar panels, which were damaged on June 25 when another Russian supply ship hit the ageing space station.

Progress also brought a razor, toothbrush and other personal items for British-American astronaut Michael Foale, whose original travel bag lies trapped behind Spektr's sealed hatch, NASA officials said.
"They have opened the hatch (to Progress) and now the main task lies in preparing to enter the damaged Spektr module," Mir flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters.

Progress, a replacement cargo ship, successfully docked with Mir on Monday under automatic pilot, but unloading had been postponed because of the need to recharge the batteries of the Kvant module where Progress is attached.
Kvant and Spektr are component parts of Mir, an orbital complex assembled in space 11 years ago.
Mir lost up to half its electric power in the June 25 collision, and a failure to beef up power supplies threatens the future of the station.

"We are working under tense conditions," Solovyov said at Mission Control. "I'd say after we carry out the operation on fully restablishing the energy supplies -- by connecting the cables to the solar panels...we'll return to standard operation proceedure."

Foale's two Russian cosmonaut colleagues, Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, will enter Spektr in spacesuits to repair the power supply, probably around July 17 or 18, although no final date has been fixed.
They will need to attach 17 internal cables to three of the four solar panels attached like wings to Spektr, no easy task in bulky spacesuits and gloves under cramped conditions, space officials say.
Experts say the fourth solar panel, which is damaged outside, probably cannot be repaired.

"As far as making the repairs, it is possible that something will not work out," Solovyov said. "Going into open space or going into the Spektr module is highly unpredictable, but we are trying to foresee matters here on earth."
Solovyov played down dangers highlighted by NASA officials on Monday that opening the Spektr hatch would unleash shards of broken glass and deadly chemicals from the accident.
"From opening Spektr, we don't expect anything other than a a few flying objects," Solovyov said.
Foale will sit in the Soyuz escape capsule for safety during the repair work, which is expected to last up to four hours.
The Russian Mir station was damaged on June 25 when, under manual control of the Mir cosmonauts, it collided with a cargo ship sent up to resupply it.
Viktor Blagov, deputy flight director, told Reuters, it would take up to three days to finish unloading Progress. "Unloading is a routine operation and everything is proceeding normally," he said.
Solovyov said Foale has resumed his biological experiments under a NASA programme. The crew had to stop all scientific work after the accident.
